title: Stochastic Voronoi Ensembles for Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection methods struggle with data exhibiting varying local densities, where distance-based methods miss local anomalies and density-based methods require careful parameter selection and incur quadratic time complexity. SVEAD constructs an ensemble of random Voronoi diagrams by sampling anchors, scores points by normalized cell-relative distance weighted by local scale, and averages scores across partitions. Across 45 ADBench datasets it achieves the highest average AUC-ROC (0.8538) and AUC-PR (0.5000) among 12 baselines, including 0.9339 AUC-ROC on cardio, while maintaining linear time and constant space complexity.

Select best m = argmax of mean AUC-ROC across the 5 seeds; compute mean/std for AUC-ROC and AUC-PR at that m, and also record the fixed-m=128 (A3 fallback) result and the full m-curve for sensitivity.

Write reproduce.py: load data from cache, reuse or regenerate results/raw_cardio.json, run selection, then write results/metrics.json with (a) C1 value vs 0.9339 with the 0.0189 band and PASS/FAIL verdict, (b) C2 value vs 0.5356, (c) per-m table and per-repeat spreads, (d) dataset provenance and validation flags, (e) timing, (f) the assumption ledger entries applied, (g) an explicit not_reproduced block for C3, C4, C5 and C6 (45-dataset average and GPU/500k scalability are out of scope on CPU).

Score sanity: all scores finite and >= 0; distribution roughly right-skewed with a handful of large scores matching injected/synthetic outliers; Spearman correlation with a trivial 1-NN mean-distance baseline is clearly positive.

Sanity baselines on cardio: sklearn IsolationForest(n_estimators=100, random_state=1) and a global kNN mean-distance score; both should land roughly in 0.65-0.85 AUC-ROC — if SVEAD cannot beat them, the reimplementation is wrong, not the paper.

Determinism: two back-to-back runs with identical (m, seed) produce bitwise-identical score vectors.

Stochastic Voronoi Ensembles for Anomaly Detection
Yang Cao 1 2 Sikun Yang 2 Xuyun Zhang 3 Yujiu Yang 1
Abstract
Anomaly detection aims to identify data instances
that deviate significantly from majority of data,
which has been widely used in fraud detection,
network security, and industrial quality control.
Existing methods struggle with datasets exhibit-
ing varying local densities: distance-based meth-
ods miss local anomalies, while density-based
approaches require careful parameter selection
and incur quadratic time complexity. We observe
that local anomalies, though indistinguishable un-
der global analysis, become conspicuous when
the data space is decomposed into restricted re-
gions and each region is examined independently.
Leveraging this geometric insight, we propose
SVEAD (Stochastic Voronoi Ensembles Anomaly
Detector), which constructs ensemble random
Voronoi diagrams and scores points by normalized
cell-relative distances weighted by local scale.
The proposed method achieves linear time com-
plexity and constant space complexity. Experi-
ments on 45 datasets demonstrate that SVEAD
outperforms 12 state-of-the-art approaches.
1. Introduction
Anomaly detection is the task of identifying instances that
deviate significantly from the majority of data, which has
been a fundamental problem in machine learning with appli-
cations spanning fraud detection, network security, medical
diagnosis, and industrial quality control (Chandola et al.,
2009; Liu et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2024a;c). The central
challenge lies in distinguishing outliers from natural varia-
tions when data exhibits heterogeneous structures, multiple
clusters, or varying densities.
Existing detection strategies face complementary limita-
tions. Distance-based methods (Angiulli & Pizzuti, 2002)

efficiently identify global outliers but fail to detect anoma-
lies in regions with varying local densities, as they apply

Voronoi diagrams via anchor sampling
We adopt a sampling-based approach that constructs implicit
Voronoi diagrams efficiently, Figure 2 shows the anchor
sampling and voronoi diagram ensembles.
Anchor Sampling. For each partition, we randomly sample
m points from the dataset X without replacement to form
an anchor set A = {a1, a2, . . . , am} where m ≪n. These
anchors serve as generators for the Voronoi diagrams. The
sampling is performed uniformly, ensuring that dense re-
gions naturally receive more anchors due to higher point
concentration, while sparse regions receive fewer anchors.
This automatic density adaptation occurs without explicit
density estimation.
Voronoi Cell Assignment. Given anchor set A, the Voronoi
cell Ci associated with anchor ai is defined as:
Ci = {x ∈X : ∥x −ai∥≤∥x −aj∥, ∀j̸ = i}
(1)
where ∥· ∥denotes the Euclidean distance. Each point

partition {C1, C2, . . . , Cm} that satisfies two properties:
(1) Sm
i=1 Ci = X, ensuring complete coverage, and (2)
Ci ∩Cj = ∅for i̸ = j, ensuring exclusivity. Unlike ex-
plicit Voronoi diagram construction, we do not compute
cell boundaries or vertices; we only determine point-to-cell
membership through nearest-anchor queries.
Ensemble Construction. A single random partition may be
unstable, as different anchor samples can produce vastly dif-
ferent cell configurations. To achieve robustness, we repeat
the sampling and partitioning process t times, generating an
ensemble of diagrams {P(1), P(2), . . . , P(t)} where each
P(k), k ∈1 . . . t represents the k-th partition with its own
anchor set A(k) and cell assignment. Each partition provides
an independent view of the data’s local structure. Points
that consistently appear far from anchors across multiple
partitions are more likely to be genuine anomalies, while
random fluctuations in individual partitions are averaged
out.

4.4. Algorithm and Complexity Analysis
Algorithm Description. Algorithm 1 presents the complete
procedure of SVEAD. The algorithm consists of two phases:
ensemble construction and anomaly scoring. In the construc-
tion phase (lines 1-10), we generate t random partitions. For
each partition, we sample m anchors uniformly from the
dataset and assign each point to its nearest anchor, comput-
ing cell statistics including maximum and mean distances.
In the scoring phase (lines 11-18), we iterate through all
points and partitions, computing within-cell scores using
the dual-factor formula and averaging across partitions to
obtain final anomaly scores.
Time Complexity. We analyze the computational cost for
each algorithmic component:
Partition construction (lines 1-10): Sampling m anchors

requires O(m) time. For each of n points, finding the near-
est anchor among m candidates requires O(md) operations
where d is the feature dimensionality, taking O(nmd) in
total. Constructing one partition thus requires O(nmd), and
building t partitions costs O(nmdt).
6


=== page 7 ===
Stochastic Voronoi Ensemble for Anomaly Detection
Score computation (lines 11-19): For each point and each
partition, we recompute the cell assignment by finding the
nearest anchor, requiring O(md) operations. Computing
the score requires O(d). Processing all points across all
partitions requires O(nmdt) operations.
The total time complexity is O(nmdt) + O(nmdt) =
O(nmdt), which simplifies to O(mnt) when d is treated as
a constant or is small relative to n. Since m ≪n in practice,
this scales linearly with dataset size.
Space Complexity. The algorithm stores anchor sets across
t partitions requiring O(tmd) space, and cell statistics (δmax
and δmean) for m cells per partition requiring O(tm) space.
The total space complexity is O(tmd + tm) = O(tmd),
which simplifies to O(tm) when d is constant. Excluding
the input dataset itself, the algorithm’s memory footprint is
O(tm), where t and m are constant hyperparameters, thus
SVEAD’s space complexity is constant.
5. Experiments
This section conducts a comprehensive evaluation with the
existing state-of-the-art methods to empirically verify the
effectiveness and efficiency of SVEAD. Our evaluation cov-
ers a wide range of datasets, including synthetic datasets
with different anomaly types and 45 real-world datasets.
5.1. Experimental Setup
Datasets. We evaluate SVEAD on 45 publicly available
benchmark datasets widely used in anomaly detection from
ADBench (Han et al., 2022). These datasets span diverse
domains including medical diagnosis, network security, im-
age recognition, and industrial monitoring, with varying
characteristics in terms of dimensionality (ranging from 3 to
1,555 features), sample size (from 80 to 619,326 instances),

and anomaly ratio (from 0.17% to 34.99%).
Baseline Methods. We compare SVEAD against 12 state-
of-the-art anomaly detection methods spanning different
paradigms: traditional methods including LOF (Breunig
et al., 2000), Isolation Forest (Liu et al., 2008), iNNE (Ban-

Algorithm Description. Algorithm 1 presents the complete
procedure of SVEAD. The algorithm consists of two phases:
ensemble construction and anomaly scoring. In the construc-
tion phase (lines 1-10), we generate t random partitions. For

each partition, we sample m anchors uniformly from the
dataset and assign each point to its nearest anchor, comput-
ing cell statistics including maximum and mean distances.
In the scoring phase (lines 11-18), we iterate through all
points and partitions, computing within-cell scores using
the dual-factor formula and averaging across partitions to
obtain final anomaly scores.
Time Complexity. We analyze the computational cost for
each algorithmic component:
Partition construction (lines 1-10): Sampling m anchors
requires O(m) time. For each of n points, finding the near-
est anchor among m candidates requires O(md) operations
where d is the feature dimensionality, taking O(nmd) in
total. Constructing one partition thus requires O(nmd), and
building t partitions costs O(nmdt).

```python
def sample_anchors(n, m, rng):

def assign_cells(X, A, chunk_rows=4096):
    # returns cell (int32), delta (float64)
    n = X.shape[0]; m = A.shape[0]
    cell = np.empty(n, np.int32); delta = np.empty(n, np.float64)
    A2 = (A*A).sum(1)
    for

s in range(0, n, chunk_rows):

        Xb = X[s:e]
        # dist^2 = |x|^2 - 2 x.a + |a|^2
        d2 = (Xb*Xb).sum(1)[:,None] - 2.0 * (Xb @ A.T) + A2[None,:]
        np.maximum(d2, 0, out=d2)
        j = np.argmin(d2, axis=1)   # lowest index on ties
        cell[s:e] = j
        delta[s:e] = np.sqrt(d2[np.arange(e-s), j])
    return cell, delta
```

Target dataset (paper Table 3): cardio, 1831 samples, 21 features, 176 anomalies
(9.61%), Healthcare category.

Resolution order (first success wins):

std 1), so no further scaling is applied when it is used.  For the OpenML

"""

import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

)
ADBENCH_URL_MIRRORS = [
    ADBENCH_URL,
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Minqi824/ADBench/master/"
    "adbench/datasets/Classical/6_cardio.npz",
    "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/Minqi824/ADBench@main/"
    "adbench/datasets/Classical/6_cardio.npz",

CTG_FEATURES = [
    "LB", "AC", "FM", "UC", "DL", "DS", "DP", "ASTV", "MSTV", "ALTV", "MLTV",
    "Width", "Min", "Max", "Nmax", "Nzeros", "Mode", "Mean", "Median",
    "Variance", "Tendency",
]

WORKSPACE_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
LOCAL_DIR = WORKSPACE_ROOT / "data"
LOCAL_NPZ = LOCAL_DIR / "cardio_adbench.npz"


def _cache_dir() -> Path:
    p = os.environ.get("REPRO_DATA_CACHE")

    checks = {

    d = np.load(path)
    X = np.asarray(d["X"], dtype=np.float64)

def _download_adbench(dest: Path) -> Path:
    import requests

    last_err = None
    for url in ADBENCH_URL_MIRRORS:
        try:
            r = requests.get(url, timeout=120)
            if r.status_code == 200 and len(r.content) > 1000:
                dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                tmp = dest.with_suffix(".part")
                tmp.write_bytes(r.content)
                tmp.replace(dest)
                return dest
            last_err = f"{url} -> HTTP {r.status_code}"
        except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover - network dependent
            last_err = f"{url} -> {exc!r}"

    """Fallback: OpenML cardiotocography (UCI CTG), same filter as ADBench."""

"""Core SVEAD algorithm (paper Section 4, Algorithm 1), reimplemented.

Per partition k = 1..t:
  * sample m anchors uniformly from X without replacement        (R1, A4)
  * assign every point to its nearest anchor in Euclidean space  (R2/R11/Eq.1)
  * per cell: delta_max, delta_mean over all members             (R4, Alg.1 l.7-10)
  * per point: s = (delta / delta_max) * delta_mean              (R3, Eq.2-3)
    - a cell holding only its anchor is skipped in that partition (R5)
Final score = arithmetic mean over the t partitions               (R6, Eq.5)
Time is O(n*m*d*t) with chunked distance blocks                   (R12).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np

CHUNK_ROWS = 2048


@dataclass
class PartitionStats:
    cell_ids: np.ndarray
    delta: np.ndarray
    cell_max: np.ndarray
    cell_mean: np.ndarray
    cell_count: np.ndarray
    valid: np.ndarray  # points scored in this partition
    anchor_idx: np.ndarray = field(default=None)


def sample_anchors(n: int, m: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """Uniform sampling without replacement (requirement R1).

    numpy's Generator.choice(..., replace=False) is uniform over subsets; the
    finite-population correction of the naive sequential draw is not used, so
    the sample is uniform by construction (assumption A4).
    """
    if m > n:
        raise ValueError(f"m={m} exceeds n={n}")
    idx = rng.choice(n, size=m, replace=False)
    return np.sort(idx)


def assign_cells(X: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray, chunk_rows: int = CHUNK_ROWS):
    """Nearest-anchor membership + distance, implicit Voronoi (R2, R11).

    Returns (cell_ids int32 (n,), delta float64 (n,)).  numpy.argmin breaks
    ties towards the lowest anchor index (assumption A5).  No cell boundaries
    are ever materialised.
    """
    n = X.shape[0]
    m = A.shape[0]
    cell = np.empty(n, dtype=np.int32)
    delta = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    a_sq = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", A, A)
    for s in range(0, n, chunk_rows):
        e = min(n, s + chunk_rows)
        Xb = X[s:e]
        # ||x - a||^2 = ||x||^2 - 2 x.a + ||a||^2
        d2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", Xb, Xb)[:, None] - 2.0 * (Xb @ A.T) + a_sq[None, :]
        np.maximum(d2, 0.0, out=d2)
        j = np.argmin(d2, axis=1).astype(np.int32)
        cell[s:e] = j
        delta[s:e] = np.sqrt(d2[np.arange(e - s), j])
    return cell, delta


def partition_stats(X: np.ndarray, anchors: np.ndarray,
                    chunk_rows: int = CHUNK_ROWS) -> PartitionStats:
    """One random Voronoi partition: assignment + per-cell statistics."""
    m = anchors.shape[0]
    cell, delta = assign_cells(X, X[anchors], chunk_rows=chunk_rows)
    count = np.bincount(cell, minlength=m).astype(np.int64)
    dsum = np.bincount(cell, weights=delta, minlength=m)
    cell_mean = np.where(count > 0, dsum / np.maximum(count, 1), 0.0)
    cell_max = np.zeros(m, dtype=np.float64)
    np.maximum.at(cell_max, cell, delta)
    # R5: cells containing only the anchor are skipped in this partition.
    valid = (count[cell] > 1) & (cell_max[cell] > 0.0)
    return PartitionStats(cell_ids=cell, delta=delta, cell_max=cell_max,
                          cell_mean=cell_mean, cell_count=count, valid=valid,
                          anchor_idx=anchors)


def score_partition(ps: PartitionStats) -> np.ndarray:
    """s = (delta / delta_max) * delta_mean ; NaN where the point is skipped (R3,R5)."""
    s = np.full(ps.delta.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float64)
    j = ps.cell_ids
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        val = (ps.delta / ps.cell_max[j]) * ps.cell_mean[j]
    s[ps.valid] = val[ps.valid]
    return s


def svead_score(X: np.ndarray, m: int, t: int = 100, seed: int = 0,
                chunk_rows: int = CHUNK_ROWS, anchor_seed_offset: int = 1000,
                skipped_as_zero: bool = False, diagnostics: bool = True):
    """Full ensemble anomaly score for X.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : (n, d) float64 array (already on the intended scale).
    m : anchors per partition.
    t : ensemble size (paper fixes t=100).
    seed : run seed; the anchor generator is seeded with seed + 1000*m so every
        (m, seed) pair is independent and reproducible (assumption A4).
    skipped_as_zero : if False (default) a point skipped by a partition is
        excluded from that partition's average (nanmean, "rely on the other
        t-1 partitions"); if True, Algorithm 1 line 20 is followed literally and
        the sum is divided by t.  Reported as a sensitivity check.

    Returns (scores (n,) float64 >= 0, diag dict).
    """
    n = X.shape[0]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(int(seed) + int(anchor_seed_offset) * int(m))
    total = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.float64)
    counts = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int64)
    n_skipped_total = 0
    cell_sizes_all = []
    for _ in range(t):
        anchors = sample_anchors(n, m, rng)
        ps = partition_stats(X, anchors, chunk_rows=chunk_rows)
        s = score_partition(ps)
        ok = ps.valid
        total[ok] += s[ok]
        counts[ok] += 1
        n_skipped_total += int((~ok).sum())
        if diagnostics:
            cell_sizes_all.append(ps.cell_count)
    if skipped_as_zero:
        scores = total / float(t)
    else:
        denom = np.where(counts > 0, counts, 1)
        scores = total / denom
    # every point skipped by every partition -> score 0 (assumption A7)
    scores[counts == 0] = 0.0
    diag = {
        "n": int(n), "m": int(m), "t": int(t), "seed": int(seed),
        "skipped_fraction": float(n_skipped_total / (n * t)),
        "points_never_scored": int((counts == 0).sum()),
        "mean_partitions_used": float(counts.mean()),
    }
    if diagnostics:
        cs = np.concatenate(cell_sizes_all)
        diag.update({
            "cells_total": int(cs.size),
            "singleton_cells": int((cs == 1).sum()),
            "singleton_cell_fraction": float((cs == 1).mean()),

"""Cardio protocol: grid-search m, 5 seeded repeats, t=100 (requirements R7, R8).

Writes (into results/):
  raw_cardio.json   per-(m, seed) records
  per_m_table.csv   same records as a flat table
  baselines.json    IsolationForest / kNN sanity baselines (intermediate check 6)

Usage:  python experiments/run_cardio.py [--quick] [--t 100] [--results DIR]
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from svead.data import load_cardio                       # noqa: E402
from svead.metrics import auc_pr, auc_pr_trapz, roc_auc  # noqa: E402
from svead.svead_core import kth_nn_distance, svead_score  # noqa: E402

M_GRID = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]   # {2^1, ..., 2^8} (R7)
SEEDS = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]                    # 5 repeats (R8, assumption A4)
T_DEFAULT = 100                            # ensemble size fixed at 100 (R7)


def run_grid(X, y, m_grid, seeds, t, verbose=True):
    records = []
    for m in m_grid:
        for seed in seeds:
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            scores, diag = svead_score(X, m=m, t=t, seed=seed)
            secs = time.perf_counter() - t0
            rec = {
                "m": int(m), "seed": int(seed), "t": int(t),
                "auc_roc": roc_auc(scores, y),
                "auc_pr": auc_pr(scores, y),
                "auc_pr_trapz": auc_pr_trapz(scores, y),
                "seconds": secs,
                "skipped_fraction": diag["skipped_fraction"],
                "singleton_cell_fraction": diag["singleton_cell_fraction"],
                "mean_cell_size": diag["mean_cell_size"],
                "max_cell_size": diag["max_cell_size"],
                "points_never_scored": diag["points_never_scored"],
                "mean_partitions_used": diag["mean_partitions_used"],
            }
            records.append(rec)
            if verbose:
                print(f"  m={m:4d} seed={seed} AUC-ROC={rec['auc_roc']:.4f} "
                      f"AUC-PR={rec['auc_pr']:.4f} ({secs:.2f}s)")
    return records


def summarize_records(records, t):
    """Per-m mean/std over the repeats."""
    per_m = {}
    for m in sorted({r["m"] for r in records}):
        rs = [r for r in records if r["m"] == m]
        per_m[m] = {
            "m": m,
            "n_repeats": len(rs),
            "t": t,
            "auc_roc_mean": float(np.mean([r["auc_roc"] for r in rs])),
            "auc_roc_std": float(np.std([r["auc_roc"] for r in rs], ddof=1)),
            "auc_roc_values": [r["auc_roc"] for r in rs],
            "auc_pr_mean": float(np.mean([r["auc_pr"] for r in rs])),
            "auc_pr_std": float(np.std([r["auc_pr"] for r in rs], ddof=1)),
            "auc_pr_values": [r["auc_pr"] for r in rs],
            "auc_pr_trapz_mean": float(np.mean([r["auc_pr_trapz"] for r in rs])),
            "seconds_mean": float(np.mean([r["seconds"] for r in rs])),
            "skipped_fraction_mean": float(np.mean([r["skipped_fraction"] for r in rs])),
            "singleton_cell_fraction_mean": float(
                np.mean([r["singleton_cell_fraction"] for r in rs])),
        }
    return per_m


def baselines(X, y, seeds=range(5)):
    """Sanity baselines on cardio (intermediate check 6)."""
    from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

    out = {"isolation_forest": [], "knn5_mean_distance": None}
    for s in seeds:
        mdl = IsolationForest(n_estimators=100, random_state=s).fit(X)
        out["isolation_forest"].append(roc_auc(-mdl.score_samples(X), y))
    out["isolation_forest_mean"] = float(np.mean(out["isolation_forest"]))
    out["isolation_forest_std"] = float(np.std(out["isolation_forest"], ddof=1))
    knn = kth_nn_distance(X, k=5)
    out["knn5_mean_distance"] = roc_auc(knn, y)
    return out


def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--quick", action="store_true",
                    help="reduced protocol: m in {2,8,32,128}, 3 seeds")
    ap.add_argument("--t", type=int, default=T_DEFAULT)
    ap.add_argument("--results", default=str(ROOT / "results"))
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    m_grid = [2, 8, 32, 128] if args.quick else M_GRID
    seeds = [1, 2, 3] if args.quick else SEEDS
    out_dir = Path(args.results)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    X, y, prov = load_cardio()
    assert X.shape == (1831, 21) and int(y.sum()) == 176, prov

    wall = time.perf_counter() - t_start
    per_m = summarize_records(records, args.t)

    base = baselines(X, y)
    print(f"[baselines] IsolationForest mean AUC-ROC {base['isolation_forest_mean']:.4f}, "
          f"kNN(5) mean-distance {base['knn5_mean_distance']:.4f}")

    payload = {
        "dataset": "cardio (ADBench, 1831x21, 176 anomalies, 9.61%)",
        "m_grid": m_grid, "seeds": seeds, "t": args.t,
        "n_repeats": len(seeds),
        "search_wall_seconds": wall,
        "data_provenance": prov,
        "per_m": {str(k): v for k, v in per_m.items()},
        "records": records,
        "baselines": base,
        "reduced_protocol": bool(args.quick),
    }
    (out_dir / "raw_cardio.json").write_text(json.dumps(payload, indent=2))

    with (out_dir / "per_m_table.csv").open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write("m,seed,t,auc_roc,auc_pr,auc_pr_trapz,seconds,skipped_fraction,"

        for r in records:

6. Conclusion
We propose SVEAD that leverages stochastic Voronoi dia-
gram and ensemble averaging for anomaly detection. The
core contribution lies in recognizing that local anomalies,
though indistinguishable under global analysis, become con-
spicuous when the data space is decomposed into restricted

spatial regions. By randomly sampling anchors to induce
Voronoi partitions and scoring points through normalized
cell-relative distances weighted by local scale, SVEAD
achieves density adaptation without explicit parameter tun-
ing. Theoretical analysis establishes that random anchor
sampling provides density-adaptive partitioning, ensemble
averaging reduces variance and ensures robustness, and
the dual-factor scoring mechanism creates clear separation
between anomalous and normal instances. Extensive experi-
ments on 45 benchmark datasets demonstrate that SVEAD
achieves state-of-the-art performance with linear time com-
plexity, outperforming 12 baselines. SVEAD’s effectiveness
across global, local, and dependency anomaly types, com-
bined with its computational efficiency, makes it a practical
solution for large-scale anomaly detection applications.

Only nearest-anchor queries are performed; no Voronoi cells, boundaries or vertices are constructed anywhere in svead/svead_core.py.

Distance computation is chunked (CHUNK_ROWS=2048) giving O(n*m*d) per partition and O(n*m*d*t) overall; the 500k x 10 probe at t=100 runs in a single-digit number of seconds and per-seed cardio timings are logged.

divergence_causes: randomness (A4: the paper states no seed policy; seeds 1-5 were chosen instead)
paper_underspecified (A3, A10: the m value used for cardio and the grid-search selection criterion are not reported)
paper_underspecified (A2, A9, A11: feature scaling and the absence of a train/test split are not stated; the ADBench pre-standardised artifact and full-data scoring were adopted)
